body_markdown:
OpenCode is an open-source terminal coding agent that talks to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Nutanix Agent Gateway provides a centralized access path for configured Nutanix Enterprise AI models and approved provider connections. Put the two together, and developers can continue using OpenCode while administrators manage model access, credential handling, and available usage information through a centrally configured endpoint. But there is a catch with the OpenCode out-of-the-box configuration: it grants access to model providers that your organization may not allow.


OpenCode Integration with Nutanix Agent Gateway


In this short blog, you’ll learn how to configure OpenCode to use Nutanix Enterprise AI (NAI) as the permitted provider path in this example.


## What OpenCode and the Nutanix Agent Gateway each do


OpenCode runs in your terminal, IDE, or desktop, reads your project, edits files, and runs commands. Under the hood, it is a client. You point it at a model provider, and it sends the conversation there.


Nutanix Agent Gateway is the unified model endpoint NAI exposes. It is OpenAI-compatible, so anything that can talk to OpenAI can talk to it. You get a single address for every approved model, a key you issue and revoke per client, and a policy layer that determines which models a key can access. The upstream frontier provider keys never leave NAI, so you can revoke access without affecting anyone’s third-party provider accounts. The gateway also counts and limits usage per key, making token usage visible.


## Prerequisites


All the examples in this blog have been tested in a Linux environment. On Mac and Windows, the same steps apply, but some directories and commands may differ.


1. Install OpenCode Terminal. Use the[official installer](https://opencode.ai/download) or a package manager, then confirm the version.


```text
opencode --version
```


1. Create an API key in Nutanix Agent Gateway, scoped to the Unified Endpoint you want to use.
2. Check that you can reach the gateway before you touch OpenCode, so you know the problem is not in the config.


```text
export NAI_FQDN="nai.example.com"                  # replace with your gateway FQDN
export NAI_BASE_URL="https://${NAI_FQDN}/enterpriseai/gateway/v1"
export NAI_API_KEY="<key copied from API Client Keys>"


curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
-H "Authorization: Bearer ${NAI_API_KEY}" \
"${NAI_BASE_URL}/models"
```


Any HTTP status back, even a 401 or a 404, tells you that TLS and the network path are fine. If you get a connection error or a certificate warning instead, fix networking or CA trust before you go further.


1. If your gateway uses an internal CA, trust it. OpenCode is a Node application and honors` NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` :


```text
export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
```


## Configure the Unified Endpoint as a provider


When configuring OpenCode in an enterprise, it is important to prioritize security. The first step is to understand how OpenCode processes configurations depending on their locations:


- Configuration files are merged together, not replaced.
- You can check the full precedence order in the[official documentation](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/config/#locations) . But the most common config locations, ordered from least to highest priority, are:


1. Global config. This is where the user preferences are. It’s a hidden folder in the user’s directory (` ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` )
2. Project config. This is where your project-specific settings are. It’s an` opencode.json` file in the root directory of your project, and it takes precedence over the global one.
3. The managed config. This is the one managed by the IT team and has the highest priority. Here, you should lock things like providers and MCPs (` /etc/opencode/opencode.json` ). Check the list of paths in the[official documentation](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/config/#locations) .


If you are just testing OpenCode with Nutanix Agent Gateway, you are okay with hosting the configuration file in your user home directory.


```text
mkdir -p ~/.config/opencode
touch ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json
```


If you are distributing OpenCode within your organization, in addition to allowing users to configure certain settings in their global config, you should create a managed config that enforces your provider configuration.


```text
sudo mkdir -p /etc/opencode
sudo chmod 755 /etc/opencode
sudo touch /etc/opencode/opencode.json
sudo chmod 644 /etc/opencode/opencode.json
```


Add the following configuration to the opencode.json file, and check below what values you must update with your environment details.


```text
{
"$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
"model": "nai/my-model-id",
"providers": {
"nai": {
"package": "@opencode/ai/providers/openai-compatible",
"name": "Nutanix Enterprise AI",
"settings": {
"baseURL": "NAI_BASE_URL",
"apiKey": "{env:NAI_API_KEY}"
},
"models": {
"my-model-id": {
"name": "My Model Display Name",
"limit": {
"context": 262144,
"output": 32768
}
}
}
}
}
}
```


Here is what each field does.


- **provider -> “nai”** is the provider ID. Any string works, but it must match everywhere else you use it, including` --model nai/...` .
- **npm** is the AI SDK package. Use` @ai-sdk/openai-compatible` when your Nutanix Agent Gateway Unified Endpoint speaks` /v1/chat/completions` .
- **options.baseURL** is the gateway base. Set` NAI_BASE_URL` to` https://<NAI_FQDN>/enterpriseai/gateway/v1` . The` /enterpriseai/gateway/v1` prefix is required. Don’t include` /chat/completions` in the base URL.
- **options.apiKey** is the credential.` {env:NAI_API_KEY}` substitutes the environment variable at load time, so the secret stays out of the file. If the variable is unset, it becomes an empty string, so export it before you launch OpenCode.
- **models** is a map of model IDs. The key must match the exact model name configured on the Unified Endpoint. OpenCode uses[Models.dev](https://models.dev/) to discover model settings, but because a gateway is a custom provider, there are no entries. So declare` limit.context` and` limit.output` yourself, or OpenCode cannot compute the remaining context.
- **model** at the top level is the default model, written as` provider_id/model_id` .


Export the variable in the shell that launches OpenCode. Add it to your shell profile, or source a secret-manager wrapper:


```text
export NAI_API_KEY="<key copied from API Client Keys>"
```


You can also skip the inline key and run` /connect` inside OpenCode, then pick the` nai` provider. That stores the key in` ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json` , and you can drop the` apiKey` line.


## For Private AI: lock providers to the gateway


The Nutanix Agent Gateway should be the only entry door for AI in your organization. If you chose the **managed config** , you just provided your users with a default configuration that will load when they launch OpenCode. But there is one caveat: it doesn’t stop them from adding other providers.


You want OpenCode to reach only the Nutanix Agent Gateway Unified Endpoint. OpenCode version 2 gives you` policies` for this.` provider.use` is an action that you can set in a policy to` allow` or` deny` providers.


First, you set a` provider.use` action to` deny` all the provider resources by default. Then, you set a` provider.use` action to only` allow` specific providers. It doesn’t matter whether your users add additional providers in their global config or try to override settings with environment variables. When the same value is declared in multiple places, the managed config file takes precedence.


Add the following policies to your managed opencode.json file, after the providers key.


```text
{
"$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
"model": "nai/my-model-id",
"providers": {...},


"policies": [
{
"action": "provider.use",
"resource": "*",
"effect": "deny"
},
{
"action": "provider.use",
"resource": "nai",
"effect": "allow"
}
]
}
```


Give each developer and agent their own API key instead of sharing a single key. That is what makes NAI’s per-client token rate limits meaningful, and it keeps usage attributable to each client so you can make better decisions about how to optimize your AI spend.


## Verify it works


List the models OpenCode can see.


```text
opencode models
```


Success looks like your gateway model appearing as` nai/my-model-id` . Then run a smoke test.


```text
opencode run --model nai/my-model-id "Reply with the single word: ok"
```


Success is a normal completion with no provider or auth error. To inspect the merged config and the stored credential.


```text
opencode debug config
opencode auth list
```


OpenCode does not automatically discover the model list for a custom provider, so what shows up here is the model you declared in the config. That is why the config lists the model manually instead of querying the gateway. If you’d like to try an OpenCode plugin that automatically discovers custom models, check the[opencode-model-discovery](https://github.com/yuhp/opencode-models-discovery) plugin.


## Wrap-up


You now have OpenCode talking to Nutanix Agent Gateway through one provider and one key from your secret manager. The allowlist keeps traffic on the gateway, and the policy on each key enforces the same boundary on the server side. Give every developer a scoped key, and you can attribute usage and limits to a person or agent instead of a shared account.


If you want to learn more about Nutanix Agent Gateway, don’t miss the following video and subscribe to our YouTube channel.
